questions.question: What is the DRY principle and how do you apply it?
questions.title: The DRY Principle
questions.direct_answer: DRY ('Don't Repeat Yourself') means every piece of knowledge has a single, authoritative representation: one place defines a rule, and everywhere else uses it. In practice: extract a repeated method, a shared validation, a single config constant, or a partial view — so a change lives in one place. DRY is NOT about avoiding any repetition of characters (that's over-extraction); it's about one source of truth for a concept. The opposite, WET ('Write Everything Twice' / 'We Enjoy Typing'), means a change requires edits in many places, which is where bugs creep in.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand DRY as 'one source of truth for a concept' (not 'never repeat characters') and know when to extract.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Over-extracting (DRYing unrelated things that just look similar) or blind copy-paste (the WET opposite).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: DRY = one source of truth per concept; extract a method/validation/constant/partial so a change lives in one place. Not 'never repeat characters' — over-extraction is a trap.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself — means every piece of knowledge has a single, authoritative representation: one place defines a rule, and everywhere else uses it. In practice: extract a repeated method, a shared validation, a single config constant, or a partial view, so a change lives in one place. DRY is not about avoiding any repetition of characters — that's over-extraction — it's about one source of truth for a concept. The opposite, WET, Write Everything Twice or We Enjoy Typing, means a change requires edits in many places, which is where bugs creep in because you fix it in one spot and miss the other three. A common mistake is over-extracting things that merely look similar but aren't the same concept, which is forced coupling, and confusing no repeated characters with one source of truth, which is the real DRY.

sections.title: DRY vs WET
sections.content:
One source of truth vs many copies; a change in one place vs edits everywhere.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[repeated logic] -->|DRY| O[one method; change once]
  R -->|WET| M[many copies; change everywhere; miss one -> bug]
```

sections.title: DRY in practice
sections.content:
```ruby
# WET: same validation logic in two controllers
#   validates_email(params[:email]) in SessionsController
#   validates_email(params[:email]) in UsersController

# DRY: one method, used everywhere
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  def validate_email(email)
    email.present? && email.match?(/\A[^@]+@[^@]+\z/)
  end
end
# now both controllers call validate_email; change it in one place

# DRY config: one constant
MAX_AGE = 120   # defined once, referenced everywhere

# DRY view: a partial
# app/views/shared/_error.html.erb  -> rendered from many views
#   <%= render 'shared/error', object: @user %>
```

questions.question: What is a common mistake when using Dry Principle?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Dry Principle
questions.direct_answer: A common mistake with the DRY principle and how do you apply it is using the rule without checking its boundary conditions. DRY ('Don't Repeat Yourself') means every piece of knowledge has a single, authoritative representation: one place defines a rule, and everywhere else uses it. That can make a valid-looking result fail for an empty input, a nil value, a duplicate, or a different ordering. I prevent it by naming the assumption, testing the boundary, and checking the result against a small hand-worked example.
